idiom_name: typed clone(): this for class hierarchies; structuredClone for data-only graphs
implementation_notes: At run time TypeScript is JavaScript, so structuredClone is the deep-copy primitive for data-shaped configuration objects - but its typing is an unchecked assertion (structuredClone<T>(x): T) and it strips the prototype chain, so a class instance comes back as a plain object while the compiler still believes the declared type. The type-safe realization for class hierarchies is a hand-written clone(): this (or a copy constructor returning the concrete type), which preserves both the static and the dynamic type; for plain config objects a spread ({...preset}) is the shallow copy-with-overrides idiom, and readonly/const-asserted preset types keep the literal shape checked.
pitfalls: structuredClone<T> asserts T without checking: clone a class instance and you get a plain object typed as the class - methods fail at run time while the compiler stays happy.
Only own enumerable data survives the clone; methods, private # fields, getters/setters and property descriptors are type-level illusions that disappear.
A spread copy is shallow despite the immutable-looking types: nested objects are shared, so 'cloning' a preset and mutating a nested field mutates the prototype.
